deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivation. It is a prose draft for Riemann's epistemological fragment 'Versuch einer Lehre von den Grundbegriffen der Mathematik und Physik als Grundlage für die Naturerklärung'. The previous and next pages hold drafts of its opening. The argument runs as follows.

(1) Starting point: the concept of 'things existing for themselves' (für sich bestehende Dinge) has already been formed by abstraction. This is source (1) of concepts on the previous page.

(2) Change (Veränderung) contradicts this concept. Reflecting on change therefore poses a task: keep the concept of self-subsistent things as far as possible. This is source (2) of concepts, the transformation or completion of concepts to remove contradictions. Doing so produces two new concepts at once: continuous change (stetige Veränderung) and causality (Causalität).

(3) Continuity. Observation only shows a thing passing from one state, or more generally one determination (Bestimmungsweise), to another without any perceived jump. Two hypotheses fit this:
- (a) the passage happens through a very large but finite number of jumps, each imperceptible to our senses;
- (b) the thing passes through all intermediate stages.
The strongest reason for (b) is the demand to preserve the concept of self-subsistent things. Riemann concedes that one cannot actually picture a passage through all intermediate stages. He answers that the same holds equally of all concepts.

In modern terms, (a) is a step function with many small jumps and (b) is a continuous path through the continuum of intermediate values. Experience cannot decide between them, since (a) can come arbitrarily close to (b). The choice rests on conceptual economy.

(4) Causality. From the concept of self-subsistence, confirmed in experience, one infers that a thing stays what it is unless something else is added. This is a generalized principle of persistence or inertia. Hence the drive to seek a cause for every change.

(5) The bottom note is an outline of headings, not a derivation: 'Task of explaining nature: to recognize the connection of things from the connection of appearances. Difference between appearances and things. Formation of the concept of self-subsistent things.'
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no computation.

Conceptually, the inference from the empirical absence of perceived jumps to genuine continuity is admittedly not compelled by observation. Riemann says so himself: both hypotheses (a) and (b) fit the data, and (b) is chosen on conceptual grounds. So this is a stated methodological choice, not a slip.

results.what: Origin of the concept of continuous change: of two hypotheses that fit observation equally (many imperceptible finite jumps vs. passage through all intermediate stages), continuity is adopted to preserve the concept of self-subsistent things.
results.modern_name: Epistemology of the continuum / continuity hypothesis in physics (philosophical sense, not Cantor's CH)
results.usually_credited_to: Long tradition (Leibniz's law of continuity; Herbart's treatment of change and the continuum, which Riemann explicitly follows)

results.what: Causality derived from the persistence of self-subsistent things: a thing remains what it is unless something else is added, hence every change demands a cause.
results.modern_name: Principle of causality / generalized principle of inertia
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Leibniz, Kant, Herbart; inertia from Galileo/Descartes/Newton)

results.what: Concept formation by two routes, abstraction and the revision of concepts to remove contradictions, applied to change.
results.modern_name: Riemann's (Herbartian) theory of concept formation in natural science
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, building on Herbart; the fragment is published in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (Weber/Dedekind), Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts

checkable.sympy: limit(floor(N*t)/N, N, oo) == t  (for fixed real t)
checkable.asserts: My own illustration, not on the page. A path made of N jumps of size 1/N approaches the continuous path t as N grows. This is why observation cannot separate 'very many imperceptible jumps' from 'passage through all intermediate stages'.
